desc:
Find the length of the longest string t such that t occurs in s at two start positions i < j with i + |t| ≤ j, that is, the two occurrences do not overlap. If there is no such string, return 0.

s = "banana"  ->  2   ("an" at 1 and 3; "ana" would overlap itself)
s = "aaaa"    ->  2   ("aa" at 0 and 2)
s = "abcd"    ->  0
s = "xabcyabcz" ->  3 ("abc" at 1 and 5)
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: The quadratic dynamic program over all pairs of positions is correct but needs O(n<sup>2</sup>) time, too slow when n = 6,000. Look for a property that lets you binary search the length.
If a non-overlapping repeat of length L exists, then its prefixes of length L - 1 also repeat at the same two positions, still without overlap. So the predicate is monotone in L.
For a fixed L, hash every window. Store the earliest start of each hash. A window starting at j whose hash was first seen at i with j - i ≥ L proves length L is feasible. Binary search on L.
editorial: Feasibility of length L is monotone: dropping the last character of a valid pair keeps the two occurrences at the same start positions and, with a shorter length, still non-overlapping. So we binary search L in [0, n/2] (two non-overlapping blocks need 2L ≤ n).

To test one L, compute the rolling hashes of all windows of length L. For each hash remember the smallest start index where it appeared. For a window at start j, if its hash was first seen at i and j - i ≥ L, the pair is valid. Using the earliest start is enough: if any earlier-or-equal start works, the earliest one has the largest gap. Each test is O(n), so the total is O(n log n). Hash collisions are astronomically unlikely with a 61-bit prime modulus; a robust version compares the actual substrings on a hit. The alternative O(n2) DP uses lcp[i][j] capped at j - i.
